newsitem.title: USA: U.S. trade gap soars again in January.
newsitem.headline: U.S. trade gap soars again in January.

text.p: Record imports sent the January U.S. trade deficit spiraling higher to the widest monthly gap in more than nine years, the Commerce Department said Thursday, likely putting a drag on the economy's first-quarter growth.
The January shortfall between exports and imports of goods and services shot up 21.1 percent to $12.71 billion after a revised 31.6 percent jump in December.
Commerce said the trade gap was the widest since the fourth quarter of 1987, when deficits were running at an average $12.9 billion a month.

In January, a strong U.S. economy drew in imports to meet vibrant consumer demand while struggling Europe and Japan offered a less buoyant market for American-made goods. Costly imported oil and an appreciating dollar that priced up U.S. goods for foreigners also helped tip the balance.
"It's going to get worse, not better," predicted economist Sung Won Sohn of Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis. "Trade will be a drag on the economy."

Sohn said relatively strong consumer spending likely will keep the U.S. economy growing at around a 3 percent rate in the current first quarter, but that will be down from 3.9 percent in the final quarter of 1996.

Not long after the trade report was issued, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan offered his strongest indication yet that stiffer interest rates were near, which might put a damper on the bubbling economy.

Speaking to the Joint Economic Committee of Congress, the Fed chief noted the economy was displaying "a great deal of vigor" and that it was vital to keep inflation muted for fear it might put a crimp in the expansion down the road.

The policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets next Tuesday to consider raising interest rates for the first time in more than two years. Costlier credit would raise borrowing costs for consumers and businesses and slow the economy.
Other reports Thursday underlined the durability of the long-running economic recovery, still generating jobs and wealth in its seventh year of growth since the last recession in 1990-91.
The Labour Department said that new claims for jobless pay edged up by only a modest 3,000 last week to 312,000.

The closely watched four-week moving average of claims was up to 312,250 from a revised 310,750 the week before -- a level that economist Marilyn Schaja of Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. of New York said "fit with the perception of a tight labour market."

Separately, the Federal Reserve Bank of Phildalephia said business in the region remained strong in March as its activity index rose to 21.1 from 17.4 in February. New orders eased but shipments of finished goods from factories were strong and hiring was brisk.

In the trade report, Commerce said total imports of goods and services into the United States climbed 2.2 percent to a record $83.48 billion in January, a third consecutive monthly increase. Exports fell for a second month in a row, down 0.6 percent to $70.78 billion.

The cost of imported petroleum products rose to $5.11 billion from $4.66 billion in December. The price per barrel of imported crude oil was up to $21.99 from $21.65, the highest since January 1991 during the Gulf War.
While the politically sensitive deficit with Japan edged up 0.7 percent to $4.29 billion in January, the shortfall with China accelerated 40.8 percent to $3.72 billion.
The rising bilateral deficit with China is likely to aggravate tensions between the two countries since the United States says China guards its own markets while aggressively selling overseas.
The United States typically runs a surplus on its trade with other countries in services, like travel and tourism, that partly offsets big merchandise trade deficits.

In January the merchandise deficit increased 12.7 percent to $19.02 billion from $16.87 billion in December. The surplus on services narrowed 1.1 percent to $6.31 billion from $6.38 billion in December.
The Commerce Department said there were record imports of industrial supplies and materials, capital goods and cars and parts during January.

Meanwhile, exports of U.S.-produced commercial aircraft plummeted by $869 million to their lowest level in a year while foreign sales of U.S. telecommunications equipment and capital goods also dropped sharply.
The deficit with Canada narrowed by 19.5 percent to $1.87 billion in January and with Western Europe it improved by 34.9 percent to $1.34 billion. But those were rare instances of improvement.
The gap with Mexico shot up 92.4 percent to $1.28 billion and the shortfall with Taiwan widened 48.2 percent to $1.07 billion in January, Commerce said.
